item.description:

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] US immigration agents are patrolling airports to arrest visa overstayers
item.description:
US immigration agents are patrolling airports to arrest visa overstayers

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 07/29/2026 - 20:06
This comes as June saw the highest rate of immigration detentions since Trump took power
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents confront protesters as they gather outside the federal immigration centre at Delaney Hall, where ICE is detaining immigrants in Newark, New Jersey, on 8 June 2026 (Spencer Platt/Getty Images via AFP)
Off

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are now patrolling US airports looking to arrest people who have overstayed their visas and are taking domestic flights around the country, ABC News reported on Tuesday. 

Visa overstays have typically been a civil violation rather than a criminal offence, given these are foreigners who entered the US legally. 

Many in the US also often find themselves in a risky position because their Green Card applications for US permanent residency do not get processed in time - before their visas expire. 

At least 27 people have been arrested across nine states using this strategy so far, ABC News found. ICE is using traveller data from the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), which runs airport security and scans every person who is scheduled to fly, whether domestic or international. 

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said in a statement that any visa overstayers will only be permitted to use US airports to "self-deport". 

The move comes as the Trump administration, under the new DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, aims to boost arrest numbers and meet the president's campaign goal of one million deportations a year of "illegals", or those who entered the country undocumented.

Many say they are seeking asylum, but that pathway has now largely been shut down. 

A surge

Last month, ICE had its highest number of bookings into its immigration detention facilities since Trump assumed power in January 2025.

More than 43,000 people were taken into custody to await deportation, with an average of 1,500 arrests per day in June, ICE's own data showed. 

DHS maintains that it does not have an arrest quota, but ICE agents themselves have been overheard discussing receiving bonuses if arrests surge. 

Media coverage has largely died down since Trump ended the violent Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis earlier this year, but ICE's tactics have not changed.

Agents killed two people earlier this month in Texas and Maine, neither of whom had a criminal record. 

The agents are in many cases in plainclothes with their faces and their eyes covered, prompting detainees to believe they are being kidnapped when they are suddenly tackled to the ground while working, shopping, or walking on the street. 

Social media videos of hundreds of such incidents prompted outrage across the country last year. 

They may have also changed minds. 

A Gallup poll from earlier this month showed that while 55 percent of Americans wanted to reduce immigration in 2024 - the year Trump was elected - only 30 percent feel the same now. 

The shift reverses a four-year trend, Gallup shows. 

Overall, nearly 80 percent of Americans, a record high, now say immigration is a good thing for the country. 

Temporary protected status

A key component of Trump's immigration policy has been to end temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of thousands of non-immigrants who cannot return home.

TPS is a designation for a limited period that allows non-citizens to obtain a US work permit while they await conditions to improve in their own countries, if they are deemed by the US government to be too dangerous to return to. It can be extended for up to 18 months at a time, with no overall limit set in stone.

TPS has so far been eliminated for Myanmar, Venezuela, Honduras, Nepal, Nicaragua, Afghanistan, and Cameroon. 

Haiti and Syria's designations are set to end this week, meaning citizens of those countries who have been under TPS since 2010-2011 will now be subject to arrest and detention by ICE.

There are more than 350,000 Haitians in the US on TPS, and at least 6,000 Syrians.

“Enforcement will be carried out," DHS warned in a post on X.

"You can wait for DHS to deport you or you leave now by visiting DHS.Gov/CBPHOME."

DHS has said it offers foreigners up to $2,500 in reimbursements if they use the "CBP Home" app to book their flight and leave the country of their own accord, but it's unclear if anyone has received that money.

item.description:
'Whitewashing Laura Loomer': AP interview sparks backlash on social media

The Associated Press is facing backlash after publishing an interview with Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and close ally of US President Donald Trump, during her visit to Ukraine.

The article quickly drew criticism from journalists, commentators and social media users, many of whom accused the news agency of attempting to "whitewash" one of the US's most controversial figures.

Loomer has long been one of the most polarising figures in US conservative politics, having repeatedly drawn condemnation for anti-Muslim rhetoric, racist remarks and conspiracy theories.

Critics argued that the AP's focus on her recent comments about Ukraine risked overshadowing that record and portraying her as a more conventional political figure.

item.description:
Lebanon seeks arrest of businessman accused of meeting Netanyahu

Lebanese judicial authorities issued a warrant on Wednesday seeking the arrest of influential businessman Antoun Sehnaoui, who is accused of meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid Israel's war on Lebanon.

A Lebanese judicial source told AFP that prosecutor and judge Ahmad Rami had issued a 30-day wanted notice for Sehnaoui "on charges of dealing with the Israeli enemy and violating Lebanon's boycott law against Israel".

Lebanese law criminalises contact with Israel despite the countries beginning direct talks under US sponsorship in April.

Axios journalist Barak Ravid had reported that, on Monday night in Washington, Sehnaoui and former US envoy Morgan Ortagus hosted a dinner attended by high-profile officials including Netanyahu.

An accompanying photo showing Sehnaoui, a Lebanese Christian, and Netanyahu at the same table sparked uproar on social media in Lebanon across the political spectrum.

The judicial official said that several lawyers had also submitted a report demanding "the prosecution of Sehnaoui for crimes related to dealing with Israel and communicating with Netanyahu".

The prosecutor is to examine the matter and decide whether to refer it to the military court.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Amnesty: India sent 2,596 arms shipments to Israel during genocide in Gaza
item.description:
Amnesty: India sent 2,596 arms shipments to Israel during genocide in Gaza

Submitted by Azad Essa on Wed, 07/29/2026 - 15:05
Amnesty said its 'conservative' methodology meant it was likely underestimating the true extent of India's contribution to Israel
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Indian counterpart, Narendra Modi, attend a press conference in Jerusalem, on 26 February 2026 (Gil Cohen-Magen/AFP)
Off

Indian state-owned and private companies shipped at least 2,596 consignments comprising hundreds of thousands of arms, ammunition and military components to Israel during the genocide in Gaza, a new Amnesty International report has revealed. 

The shipments, sent between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, included machine-gun components, 155 mm high-explosive artillery shells supplied to Elbit Systems, explosive warheads for the SkyStriker "kamikaze" drones - similar to those discovered amid the ruins in Khan Younis - and armoured vehicle components destined for major suppliers to the Israeli military.

According to Amnesty, these amounted to 564,970 parts of explosive ordnance (drone warheads, artillery shell casings and others); 390,516 small arms parts for military-grade weapons; and 298 components of military vehicles to large Israeli companies that supplied the Israeli armed forces.

As of 29 July 2026, at least 247,387 Palestinians have been either killed or injured since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza, following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The report, "Made in India: The Supply of Weapons and Ammunition to Israel", published on Thursday, said its findings were "based on a deliberately conservative methodology", and were likely to underestimate the "true extent of India's contribution to Israel's military supply chain".

Rising Indian complicity 

The report is the latest in a series alleging that India has materially supported Israel's genocide in Gaza, following earlier allegations that New Delhi supplied combat drones, bombs and weapons components to Israel after October 2023.

In May 2026, the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and No Harbour for Genocide (NHG) warned of a "flood" of military supplies from India to Israel. 

"Israel has a huge domestic production, but they rely on specific components, whether it's like high-end technology material for aerospace or bulk materials such as military steel," a spokesperson for No Harbour for Genocide told Middle East Eye at the time. 

Likewise, an Al Jazeera investigation based on Israeli Tax Authority (ITA) import data found that India was the second-largest exporter of military-related goods to Israel between October 2023 and October 2025. 

Israeli army reservist 'flees' India after war crimes allegation filed
Read More »

Al Jazeera noted the data likely represented only a partial picture of total arms transfers to Israel and did not establish the end use of the shipments in Gaza.

Likewise, Amnesty's investigators based their analysis on shipments classified under specific Harmonized System (HS) codes, the internationally used customs classification system for traded goods.

These included HS codes 9301–9307, which cover weapons, ammunition and their parts and accessories; and HS code 8710, which covers armoured and fighting vehicles and their components. 

Researchers excluded shipments labelled only with internal product or part numbers, where it was not possible to determine whether the items were military or civilian.

It also excluded hundreds of shipments of dual-use small-arms components, as well as weapons, parts and ammunition likely intended for anti-missile defence systems.

Amnesty said its deliberately conservative methodology meant its findings were likely to underestimate the true extent of India's contribution to Israel's military supply chain.

Nonetheless, its findings revealed there were several companies, including state-owned ventures, involved in supplying military aid to Israel.

It said it wrote to nine companies as well as the Indian state but did not receive a reply by the time of publication. 

"In light of the International Court of Justice’s provisional measures orders recognizing a plausible risk of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, the Indian authorities cannot credibly argue that they did not know that continuing to authorize and facilitate arms transfers to Israel carries a substantial risk of contributing to serious violations of international law," Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general, said in a statement. 

Callamard added that while the Israeli military continued to inflict death and suffering in Gaza, "Indian companies continued to profit by supplying components and munitions destined for Israel’s defence sector."

India-Israel defence ties

India-Israel ties have accelerated over the past decade under the leadership of Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Benjamin Netanyahu. 

India is the world's largest purchaser of Israeli weapons, and several Israeli arms manufacturers have established production facilities in the country through joint ventures with Indian companies.

Earlier this year, during Modi's visit to Israel, the two countries upgraded ties to a Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity.

The relationship has since expanded further, with a series of new memorandums of understanding (MoUs) and reports of potential defence partnerships, including discussions over India manufacturing Iron Dome interceptor missiles for Israel. 

Israel to install statue of Indian Maratha king as gesture of friendship
Read More »

Diplomatically, the Indian government has been one of Israel's staunchest supporters.

New Delhi has refused to join South Africa's case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, which alleges violations of the Genocide Convention, and has rejected calls to impose an arms embargo on Israel. 

It has also cracked down on pro-Palestine protests and activism within India.

When Indian civil society groups petitioned the Supreme Court in September 2024 to halt arms exports, the court dismissed the case, ruling that decisions on foreign policy fall within the government's domain, not the judiciary.

External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar has also maintained that India's arms exports are guided by the country's "national interest".

"The issue of India's exports, including India's exports of anything which directly or indirectly has any military implications, is guided by our national interest and by our commitments to various regimes," Jaishankar said in December 2024.

"Where Israel is concerned, it is a country with which we have a strong record of cooperation in national security. It is also a country that has stood by us at different moments when our national security was under threat," he added.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Israeli settler terrorism threatens the basics of Palestinian survival
item.description:
How Israeli settler terrorism threatens the basics of Palestinian survival

Submitted by Ghada Majadli on Tue, 07/28/2026 - 20:49
The healthcare infrastructure that sustains West Bank communities is collapsing amid accelerated settlement expansion and violent attacks
A Palestinian ambulance drives past Israeli forces in Kafr Aqab, south of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, on 27 January 2026 (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
On

In less than 24 hours last week, four Palestinians were killed and several were injured across the occupied West Bank, as settler attacks spread to multiple villages, leaving homes, vehicles and other property damaged and burned. 

In the village of Tell, southwest of Nablus, the four Palestinians were killed on Friday in a settler attack, which also resulted in the deaths of two settlers. Hours later, Israeli forces raided a Nablus hospital to arrest two Palestinians, one of whom was being treated for a gunshot wound, while military closures and checkpoints sealed off large parts of the city and surrounding villages. 

Such deaths and injuries are only the most visible manifestations of a much broader process that has been unfolding since October 2023, with consequences extending across the occupied Palestinian territories. 

Over the past few days, Palestinians requiring life-saving dialysis have been unable to reach treatment. Women in labour have been prevented from crossing military checkpoints to access hospitals, while ambulances have been blocked from reaching patients due to road closures. 

The restrictions have thus disrupted access to emergency care, further undermining the necessary conditions for Palestinian survival.

Since the Gaza war began nearly three years ago, the occupied West Bank has witnessed an unprecedented acceleration of settlement expansion and Israel’s de facto annexation, with thousands of new settler housing units approved. 

Swaths of Palestinian territory have been declared “state land”, while settler violence has reached record levels, driving the displacement of at least 45 Palestinian communities since 2023, and reshaping the West Bank’s geography. Hundreds of Palestinians have been killed. 

Detours and checkpoints

These developments are rarely understood in the context of public health. But settlement expansion, displacement, military closures and settler violence do more than reshape the political geography of the occupied West Bank; they also reshape the conditions that determine who can live safely, move freely, access healthcare, and ultimately survive. 

The reorganisation of Palestinian space is simultaneously a reordering of the conditions necessary for life and survival. 

The death of three-month-old Ahmad Zaid earlier this month was among the clearest illustrations. The infant was being rushed to hospital when his family’s passage was blocked at an Israeli military gate near Deir Ammar refugee camp, northwest of Ramallah. 

An ambulance waited on the other side as Israeli forces kept the gate closed, despite being informed of the medical emergency. Ahmad was eventually transported to the ambulance via a longer route, but he was later pronounced dead.

In the West Bank, access to care is conditional on whether a checkpoint is open, settlers are blocking a road, or soldiers permit an ambulance to pass

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), as of this month, around 12,000 Palestinians in communities west of Ramallah were effectively isolated by the cumulative closures of access routes. 

They rely on lengthy detours, dirt roads and back-to-back ambulance transfers to reach workplaces, schools and health services, while patients requiring regular treatment, such as dialysis, depend on ambulances waiting on opposite sides of military gates. Checkpoints, gates and road closures thereby determine whether patients are able to receive timely care. 

But movement restrictions are only one dimension  through which settlement expansion is becoming a public health hazard. As settler attacks intensify and new outposts expand across the occupied West Bank, entire Palestinian communities are being uprooted, with the consequences extending far beyond the loss of a home. 

Families have been separated from the social networks that provide care and support. Farmers have lost access to the agricultural lands that once sustained their livelihoods and food security. Bedouin communities have been cut off from grazing routes, water sources and essential services. 

What was once concentrated largely in Area C is increasingly extending into the heart of the occupied West Bank, reshaping Areas A and B, designated by the Oslo Accords as falling under Palestinian administration.

Growing vulnerability 

In the area where Ahmad died this month, OCHA has documented more than 60 settler attacks since early 2024, compared with just nine incidents in the preceding four years. The nearby Ein Ayoub Bedouin community was entirely displaced in August 2025, following recurrent settler attacks and access restrictions.

In addition to causing injuries and deaths, Israeli settler violence and military operations produce chronic fear, psychological distress and persistent insecurity. 

Children exposed to repeated violence carry its effects long after an attack has ended. Elderly people and those living with chronic illnesses become increasingly vulnerable when movement is unpredictable and access to care unreliable. 

Settler terrorism: Palestinians are becoming prisoners in their own homeland
Read More »

Healthcare workers themselves must navigate checkpoints, road closures and military incursions to reach hospitals and clinics. Public health, in other words, is shaped by whether people can move safely, remain connected to their communities, sustain their businesses, and live without the constant threat of violence.

This is particularly important in the Palestinian context, both in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. In Gaza, Palestinians must navigate a permit regime that renders access to healthcare contingent upon Israeli approval. Patients wait months for responses, often missing appointments; some have died before permits were issued.

In the West Bank, access to care is conditional on whether a checkpoint is open, settlers are blocking a road, or soldiers permit an ambulance to pass. Beyond access to hospitals, the wider conditions through which health is produced and sustained are being reorganised.

Too often, discussions of settlement expansion, annexation and settler violence focus exclusively on territory and international law. These dimensions are crucial, but they overlook the systematic erosion of the conditions that make it possible to live a healthy life. 

As the occupied West Bank continues to fragment under the combined weight of settlement expansion, military violence and settler attacks, so too does the infrastructure of care upon which Palestinian communities depend.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] ‘Lenin was an enemy of humanity’: Why Kyiv wants to put Cossack chief statue in place of Soviet leader
item.description:
Removal of Soviet-era statues sped up when Russia seized Crimea in 2014, and since Putin’s 2022 invasion has moved at pace as Ukrainians question their identity

Since 2013 the plinth at the bottom of Taras Shevchenko Boulevard in Kyiv has been eerily empty. The scruffy monument is daubed in white paint and graffiti. Someone has stuck a Ukrainian trident where Lenin once stood, gazing down during the years of Soviet communism. A crowd toppled the sculpture during Ukraine’s Maidan revolution, which ousted the pro-Russian government, and smashed it with sledgehammers.

In June, Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed putting a new figure on the plinth: Ivan Mazepa, a Cossack military and political leader, who broke with Moscow and fought for Ukraine’s independence. “I am certain that where Lenin fell, Mazepa will stand firm,” Zelenskyy said. He spoke next to a bust of Mazepa in the Pechersk Lavra, an ancient Kyiv monastery hit by Russian missiles.

item.description:
Losing funds should force leaders to confront their own challenges, they said, while many voiced concerns over increasing foreign influence

A quarter of young Africans believe aid cuts by the US could have a positive impact, saying that losing foreign money will force leaders to confront and solve their own challenges, according to a new survey.

In Ghana and Nigeria, almost half (41% and 40% respectively) of young people aged 18 to 24 were optimistic, with Liberia not far behind (37%). A further one in 10 (11%) young people were uncertain about the impact, according to the African Youth Survey, which interviewed almost 5,000 people across 16 of the continent’s 54 recognised countries.
